Anglo Deception

By: Jana Marx | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
Exclusive docs leaked by a whistleblower, exposing AngloGold Ashanti's lies and deception.

Summary:
AngloGold Ashanti promised to extract uranium and sulphuric acid from a new mega tailings dam they constructed back in the early 2000's. One of the plants were never built. The other one closed down after a year, leaving a mega tailings dam full of toxic mine water without the proper precautions to keep the environment and surrounding communities safe. Harmony Gold has since bought Anglo's assests and they are applying to expand the project. But what happens to the mess Anglo left them with?

Further information:
Near Klerksdorp in North West lies one of the biggest tailings dam in South Africa – some say it’s the biggest.

Major development by AngloGold Ashanti back in the early 2000’s.

The dam was designed to hold 450 tonnes of processed mine tailings in the first stage of its lifetime.

At the time it was seen as one of the biggest tailings dams in the world.

There are several mine dumps in that area.

Just a bit of background as to why this dam was built: As gold mining technology improved, AngloGold Ashanti realized that the 15 smaller tailings dams in the area contained gold residue.

They decided to expand their gold mining activities and extract gold from those tailings dams, as the underground mine workings were reaching depletion. The idea with the mega dam was to “store” the tailings of all the tailings dams in the area.

What made this project marvellous, is that Anglo wanted to clean-up the environment in the process. So contaminated mine waste water wouldn’t just be pumped into a new mega dam. The mining company wanted to construct two separate processing plants to extract sulphuric acid and uranium from the existing tailings dams. This means they would be “mining” gold, sulphuric acid and uranium – keeping the gold and getting rid of the sulphuric acid and selling the uranium.

The result? “Clean” mine waste water that could even be repurposed for eg, irrigation.

Environmental groups were very excited. Finally the mining industry was taking their responsibility towards the environment seriously.

So the construction of the dam started. Environmental impact studies were done – all based on the assumption that those two treatment plants would be constructed. The plans were approved by the then regulator, which was the Department of Agriculture, Conservation & Environment in North West.

From the docs it seem that they regulator wasn’t that strict, because everyone was planning around a “clean” tailings dam. In fact, the dam was built on the banks of the Vaal River, because after the tailings were treated, there wasn’t much left that posed a threat to the environment.

The dam wall was also not built with terraces as usual, because a clean dam didn’t pose as much of a risk as a toxic one.

Note that the North West Department’s Authorisation did include a clause, saying: “Any changes to, or deviations from, the project description set out in this authorisation must be approved in writing by the Department, before such changes or deviations may be effected”. The project description obviously includes the building of the two extra treatment plants.

Fast-forward to AngloGold’s promises:

• the uranium extraction plant was built in 2014/2015 – and then the uranium market collapsed. The plant went out of operation within a year.

• The sulphuric acid extraction plant was never built.

In 2012 there were major spillages on the adjacent farms. Mariette Liefferink lay criminal charges against AngloGold, because of it.

In 2017 there was ‘n spillage. Cyclone Dineo caused a lot of rain in the area and the dam had overflown – all hard and toxic metals right into the Vaal.

We know mines more often than not, overpromise and underdeliver, but in 2019 a new impact study revealed that “the sulphate plume (polluted underground water table) at Kareerand continues to grow at a significant rate”.

This is their heritage in SA. Not those cute slogans about caring about the environment and the communities. They came here, mined and left us with the damage.

In 2020 Harmony Gold bought AngloGold’s South African assets. It was time to renew regulatory stuff. By that time, the DMRE has taken over from the provincial departments as regulator. Everything was approved once again. In 2021 Harmony Gold applied for a new water use licence with the Department of Water and Sanitation.

The DWS flagged the issue with the dam and insisted that it gets lined.

The crux: Harmony got approvals to continue working on a site that’s currently one of the biggest environmental threats in the country. There’s a chance that Harmony doesn’t know about AngloGold’s undelivered promises, but I strongly doubt it.

AngloGold Ashanti deceived everyone (or bribed their way through) regulatory processes to make money.

These environmental crimes can land people in prison.

They have erected a tailings dam that, by the looks of the pictures I’ve seen, cannot handle the mass of polluted water it’s holding.

The groundwater is so contaminated, that farmers apparently can’t use it. The interception boreholes drilled to control the mess underground, are few and far between, and those I’ve seen, are broken or overwhelmed by all the water.

The DMRE and Water and Sanitation are either in on it, or blissfully unaware and will be sitting with egg on their faces for approving licences without proper review.

According to my source, the dam wall is also not built according to regulations for a highly toxic tailings dam. And it’s already spilling in places. If it breaks, it will be the Merriespruit Disaster times 10, because of its size. This toxic dam is right next to the Vaal River. It’s already contaminating one of SA’s most important water resources, by spilling into the Koekemoerspruit.

The Vaal River provides water to 19 million South Africans.

Press Release:


A Dam Mess
A mega tailings dam built near the Vaal River in a bid to clean up a century of residual pollutants from mine workings in the North West sounded good on paper. But why were critical parts of the plan, including the extraction of toxic substances like radioactive uranium and sulphuric acid not fulfilled? Carte Blanche takes to the air to examine the potential for the dam’s walls to be breached, and the impact of that on nearby farmland, the critical Vaal River, and the millions of people relying on it for fresh water.
Producer: Jana Marx | Presenter: Derek Watts

Script:


For four decades, Steve Hill has been farming on the Vaal River… where it becomes the border between the Free State and North West Province.

STEVE 02;06 Thirty years back, I could lay down in a shallow stream in the Vaal River and drink that water…

This farming country borders the Vaal … apart from crops, cattle, and sheep it’s also known for its picturesque wetlands…a birder’s paradise

VAAL LINK: The Vaal is a very busy river. The entire system supplies 46% of the country’s economy - around 19 million people.
But this mighty river is under threat on multiple fronts. One of those is mining.

This is a story about a fragile ecosystem; about what’s known as a tailings dam - a massive one - built next to the Vaal River.
It’s about a listed mining company allegedly paying lip service to environmental best practice…and about what some are calling a crisis waiting to happen…

Tailings dams are typically earth-filled embankment dams used to store the by-products of mining.

They dot the landscape on the iconic old Gold Reef across three provinces.

And while the industry isn’t what it used to be, many of these dams still contain unrecovered gold that becomes profitable to mine under the right conditions.

And that’s where our story begins: around a decade ago, a company called Mine Waste Solutions, wanted to re-mine 15 old tailings dams between Klerksdorp and Potchefstroom.

New mining generated new by-products – or tailings – that had to be dumped somewhere.

That “somewhere” became a spot 2km from the Vaal River. By 2009 Mine Waste Solutions got the go-ahead from government to build their mega tailings dam called Kareerand.

It made locals like Steve very nervous.

STEVE 03:10 Our big concern was what was…at the end of the day…what was gonna happen to the environment…the Vaal River as such, as a source of natural water…

The people here had good reason to be worried as they remembered Merriespruit.

In 1994, 17 residents of a sleepy Free State mining town were killed…when a tailings dam failed…

CHARLES 5;42 That's the leading cause of failures in the past in South Africa is when there have been storms.

Dr Charles MacRobert is a geotechnical engineer - basically an expert in the behaviour of soil and rocks. He explains that a storm could cause a disaster…

CHARLES 5;56 Is that what happened at Merriespruit? Yes, yes. It was a storm that caused it to overtop.

STEVE 02;35: Ons is die versekering gegee dat dié dam se uitleg en sy bou sal van so ‘n aard wees wees dat dit sal nooit gebeur nie…

SUBTITLES: We were assured that thís dam’s layout and structure would be of such a nature that it (another Merriespruit Disaster) will never happen.
Dr MacRobert says Kareerand’s walls ARE more stable because they were built to a flatter angle than usual.

But they can still overflow…and it has happened in the past after heavy rainstorms.

To get a sense of the mega dam’s scale, we took to the air with The Bateleurs, who fly in service of the environment.

CHOPPER LINK 1 00;07: So, this is it: the Kareerand tailings dam…built to a capacity of 350 million tonnes.

If this were pure water, it would fill an astonishing 140 000 Olympic-size swimming pools. But in this case, the contents are toxic.

The dam became operational around 2011 - from here it looks full to the brim.

From the dam we saw what looked like a spillage…

CHOPPER LINK 2 I can’t say how toxic it is but to me it doesn’t look like a very healthy situation.

Back on land, we’re joined by veteran environmental activist Mariette Liefferink.

Over a decade ago, concerned farmers had first roped her in to help them, after uranium-laden water from some of the 15 old tailings dams on the same compound as Kareerand, spilled into the Koekemoerspruit - a tributary of the Vaal.

MARIETTE 2;24, in fact, it was not just one spillage. There were continuous spillages from the pipelines.

As valuable as uranium can be when the price is right…when it spills, it’s toxic and radio-active and a potential health-hazard to humans.

So Mariette locked horns with the company that by then was in charge of Mine Waste Solutions - AngloGold Ashanti.

MARIETTE 2;43 We took pictures at the time. 3;04 And we then laid criminal charges at the local police station against a wide pool of persons including directors.

The charges went nowhere, but the National Nuclear Regulator did issue several directives ordering the company to clean up the mess. Ever since, Mariette has kept an eye on developments here.

But, when it came to Kareerand, AngloGold made all the right noises…

ANGLO LINK What made this project marvellous, is that AngloGold Ashanti promised to build processing plants to extract sulphuric acid and uranium from the existing dams. So the water flowing through to the mega dam would not be so contaminated.

Uranium is one of the by-products of gold mining because it’s present in the ore that’s brought to the surface. Sulphuric acid is used in the uranium extraction process.

Back in 2008, an Environmental Impact Study warned that without the extraction plants, pollution could spike. With this undertaking in place, the North West Government allowed the dam.

BUT…IF AngloGold’s plans changed - they had to get reapproval in writing.

STEVE 04:21 So what happened to that deal? It never happened. They are only taking out gold. Our investigation found that the uranium plant worked for only a short while and the sulphuric acid plant was never even built.

We also found no reapproval for the changed plans.

TRACY-LYNN 09;01 This very serious. It points to a dereliction of duty at many levels. 9;22 And the proximity of this particular facility to the Vaal River is a huge cause of concern.

Professor Tracy-Lynn Field, an environmental lawyer, says not complying with the government’s approval has dire consequences.

TRACY-LYNN 14;40 Then contravening it or not complying with it is a crime. 1;08: And the second it's unlawfully and intentionally or negligently committing an act or an omission, that significantly - that causes significant pollution or degradation.

Then AngloGold wanted to expand the mega dam.

Their own environmental tests in 2019 showed how the sulphate plume in the groundwater was growing significantly underneath the dam.

CHARLES 21:40 I think a nice way to picture a plume, is to think if you had a bowl of water, and you dropped a bit of dye into that bowl of water… 21;59 So beneath that facility, there is this plume of acids, salts, sulphates, that is spreading. 23;12 Which is serious, I would think? It definitely would be serious.

Only a year later, another study found the plumes were still threatening the Vaal.

To test whether pollution is still taking place, we sent soil samples from spots on the Mine Waste Solutions compound, to an accredited laboratory.
Wits University’s Centre for Water Research and Development who interpreted the results, found that the soil showed excessive levels of arsenic, copper, the heavy metal lead…and high levels of radioactive uranium.

MARIETTE 12;53 We must remember that these tailings storage facilities will exist for many years even after mine closure. And uranium, as we know, has an extremely long half life.

So that’s our story’s kicker: Astonishingly, despite evidence of growing pollution and what looks like unauthorised changes to the original undertakings, Kareerand is getting bigger… to more than double its size.

And AngloGold has sold off the project.

In 2020 - with the expansion planning in an advanced stage - Harmony Gold took over, and a year later the Department of Mineral Resources and Energy, or the DMRE, authorised the project.

But for locals the question remains: who will be to blame if poor management or a massive rain storm ended in another Merriespruit-type disaster?

TRACY-LYNN 4;24 Where do you find liability in this case? 4;27 The corporate actor at the coalface is Mine Waste Solutions, and the ownership of Mine Waste Solutions has changed from AngloGold Ashanti to Harmony Gold. This has just shifted administrative liability, but it hasn't shifted criminal liability.

AngloGold Ashanti declined an interview, but said in writing it had made significant progress in reducing the environmental impact from the 15 old tailings dams in the area - some of which were built even closer to the Vaal than Kareerand.

It said the spot near the Vaal had been chosen because it allowed for construction on solid rock, rather than porous and unstable ground.

Harmony Gold says it’s met all government’s requirements and that it’s committed to operating Kareerand safely, which is why it claims to have reduced the volume of water in the mega dam and improved the lining to prevent seepage.

Harmony neglected to comment specifically on what looked to us like seepage… on our fly-over.

STEVE 01:03 If we don’t have sufficient water that’s in a good state, it’s not possible to produce food for South Africa.

Steve and other locals can only wait and see.. At least those that choose to… or have no choice.

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 13 July 2022 Press Release: A Dam Mess A mega tailings dam built near the Vaal River in a bid to clean up a century of residual pollutants from mine workings in the North West sounded good on paper. But why were critical parts of the plan, including the extraction of toxic substances like radioactive uranium and sulphuric acid not fulfilled? Carte Blanche takes to the air to examine the potential for the dam’s walls to be breached, and the impact of that on nearby farmland, the critical Vaal River, and the millions of people relying on it for fresh water. Producer: Jana Marx | Presenter: Derek Watts Script: For four decades, Steve Hill has been farming on the Vaal River… where it becomes the border between the Free State and North West Province. STEVE 02;06 Thirty years back, I could lay down in a shallow stream in the Vaal River and drink that water… This farming country borders the Vaal … apart from crops, cattle, and sheep it’s also known for its picturesque wetlands…a birder’s paradise VAAL LINK: The Vaal is a very busy river. The entire system supplies 46% of the country’s economy - around 19 million people. But this mighty river is under threat on multiple fronts. One of those is mining. This is a story about a fragile ecosystem; about what’s known as a tailings dam - a massive one - built next to the Vaal River. It’s about a listed mining company allegedly paying lip service to environmental best practice…and about what some are calling a crisis waiting to happen… Tailings dams are typically earth-filled embankment dams used to store the by-products of mining. They dot the landscape on the iconic old Gold Reef across three provinces. And while the industry isn’t what it used to be, many of these dams still contain unrecovered gold that becomes profitable to mine under the right conditions. And that’s where our story begins: around a decade ago, a company called Mine Waste Solutions, wanted to re-mine 15 old tailings dams between Klerksdorp and Potchefstroom. New mining generated new by-products – or tailings – that had to be dumped somewhere. That “somewhere” became a spot 2km from the Vaal River. By 2009 Mine Waste Solutions got the go-ahead from government to build their mega tailings dam called Kareerand. It made locals like Steve very nervous. STEVE 03:10 Our big concern was what was…at the end of the day…what was gonna happen to the environment…the Vaal River as such, as a source of natural water… The people here had good reason to be worried as they remembered Merriespruit. In 1994, 17 residents of a sleepy Free State mining town were killed…when a tailings dam failed… CHARLES 5;42 That's the leading cause of failures in the past in South Africa is when there have been storms. Dr Charles MacRobert is a geotechnical engineer - basically an expert in the behaviour of soil and rocks. He explains that a storm could cause a disaster… CHARLES 5;56 Is that what happened at Merriespruit? Yes, yes. It was a storm that caused it to overtop. STEVE 02;35: Ons is die versekering gegee dat dié dam se uitleg en sy bou sal van so ‘n aard wees wees dat dit sal nooit gebeur nie… SUBTITLES: We were assured that thís dam’s layout and structure would be of such a nature that it (another Merriespruit Disaster) will never happen. Dr MacRobert says Kareerand’s walls ARE more stable because they were built to a flatter angle than usual. But they can still overflow…and it has happened in the past after heavy rainstorms. To get a sense of the mega dam’s scale, we took to the air with The Bateleurs, who fly in service of the environment. CHOPPER LINK 1 00;07: So, this is it: the Kareerand tailings dam…built to a capacity of 350 million tonnes. If this were pure water, it would fill an astonishing 140 000 Olympic-size swimming pools. But in this case, the contents are toxic. The dam became operational around 2011 - from here it looks full to the brim. From the dam we saw what looked like a spillage… CHOPPER LINK 2 I can’t say how toxic it is but to me it doesn’t look like a very healthy situation. Back on land, we’re joined by veteran environmental activist Mariette Liefferink. Over a decade ago, concerned farmers had first roped her in to help them, after uranium-laden water from some of the 15 old tailings dams on the same compound as Kareerand, spilled into the Koekemoerspruit - a tributary of the Vaal. MARIETTE 2;24, in fact, it was not just one spillage. There were continuous spillages from the pipelines. As valuable as uranium can be when the price is right…when it spills, it’s toxic and radio-active and a potential health-hazard to humans. So Mariette locked horns with the company that by then was in charge of Mine Waste Solutions - AngloGold Ashanti. MARIETTE 2;43 We took pictures at the time. 3;04 And we then laid criminal charges at the local police station against a wide pool of persons including directors. The charges went nowhere, but the National Nuclear Regulator did issue several directives ordering the company to clean up the mess. Ever since, Mariette has kept an eye on developments here. But, when it came to Kareerand, AngloGold made all the right noises… ANGLO LINK What made this project marvellous, is that AngloGold Ashanti promised to build processing plants to extract sulphuric acid and uranium from the existing dams. So the water flowing through to the mega dam would not be so contaminated. Uranium is one of the by-products of gold mining because it’s present in the ore that’s brought to the surface. Sulphuric acid is used in the uranium extraction process. Back in 2008, an Environmental Impact Study warned that without the extraction plants, pollution could spike. With this undertaking in place, the North West Government allowed the dam. BUT…IF AngloGold’s plans changed - they had to get reapproval in writing. STEVE 04:21 So what happened to that deal? It never happened. They are only taking out gold. Our investigation found that the uranium plant worked for only a short while and the sulphuric acid plant was never even built. We also found no reapproval for the changed plans. TRACY-LYNN 09;01 This very serious. It points to a dereliction of duty at many levels. 9;22 And the proximity of this particular facility to the Vaal River is a huge cause of concern. Professor Tracy-Lynn Field, an environmental lawyer, says not complying with the government’s approval has dire consequences. TRACY-LYNN 14;40 Then contravening it or not complying with it is a crime. 1;08: And the second it's unlawfully and intentionally or negligently committing an act or an omission, that significantly - that causes significant pollution or degradation. Then AngloGold wanted to expand the mega dam. Their own environmental tests in 2019 showed how the sulphate plume in the groundwater was growing significantly underneath the dam. CHARLES 21:40 I think a nice way to picture a plume, is to think if you had a bowl of water, and you dropped a bit of dye into that bowl of water… 21;59 So beneath that facility, there is this plume of acids, salts, sulphates, that is spreading. 23;12 Which is serious, I would think? It definitely would be serious. Only a year later, another study found the plumes were still threatening the Vaal. To test whether pollution is still taking place, we sent soil samples from spots on the Mine Waste Solutions compound, to an accredited laboratory. Wits University’s Centre for Water Research and Development who interpreted the results, found that the soil showed excessive levels of arsenic, copper, the heavy metal lead…and high levels of radioactive uranium. MARIETTE 12;53 We must remember that these tailings storage facilities will exist for many years even after mine closure. And uranium, as we know, has an extremely long half life. So that’s our story’s kicker: Astonishingly, despite evidence of growing pollution and what looks like unauthorised changes to the original undertakings, Kareerand is getting bigger… to more than double its size. And AngloGold has sold off the project. In 2020 - with the expansion planning in an advanced stage - Harmony Gold took over, and a year later the Department of Mineral Resources and Energy, or the DMRE, authorised the project. But for locals the question remains: who will be to blame if poor management or a massive rain storm ended in another Merriespruit-type disaster? TRACY-LYNN 4;24 Where do you find liability in this case? 4;27 The corporate actor at the coalface is Mine Waste Solutions, and the ownership of Mine Waste Solutions has changed from AngloGold Ashanti to Harmony Gold. This has just shifted administrative liability, but it hasn't shifted criminal liability. AngloGold Ashanti declined an interview, but said in writing it had made significant progress in reducing the environmental impact from the 15 old tailings dams in the area - some of which were built even closer to the Vaal than Kareerand. It said the spot near the Vaal had been chosen because it allowed for construction on solid rock, rather than porous and unstable ground. Harmony Gold says it’s met all government’s requirements and that it’s committed to operating Kareerand safely, which is why it claims to have reduced the volume of water in the mega dam and improved the lining to prevent seepage. Harmony neglected to comment specifically on what looked to us like seepage… on our fly-over. STEVE 01:03 If we don’t have sufficient water that’s in a good state, it’s not possible to produce food for South Africa. Steve and other locals can only wait and see.. At least those that choose to… or have no choice.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Exclusive docs leaked by a whistleblower, exposing AngloGold Ashanti's lies and deception.
metadata.Summary: AngloGold Ashanti promised to extract uranium and sulphuric acid from a new mega tailings dam they constructed back in the early 2000's. One of the plants were never built. The other one closed down after a year, leaving a mega tailings dam full of toxic mine water without the proper precautions to keep the environment and surrounding communities safe. Harmony Gold has since bought Anglo's assests and they are applying to expand the project. But what happens to the mess Anglo left them with?
metadata.Further information: Near Klerksdorp in North West lies one of the biggest tailings dam in South Africa – some say it’s the biggest. Major development by AngloGold Ashanti back in the early 2000’s. The dam was designed to hold 450 tonnes of processed mine tailings in the first stage of its lifetime. At the time it was seen as one of the biggest tailings dams in the world. There are several mine dumps in that area. Just a bit of background as to why this dam was built: As gold mining technology improved, AngloGold Ashanti realized that the 15 smaller tailings dams in the area contained gold residue. They decided to expand their gold mining activities and extract gold from those tailings dams, as the underground mine workings were reaching depletion. The idea with the mega dam was to “store” the tailings of all the tailings dams in the area. What made this project marvellous, is that Anglo wanted to clean-up the environment in the process. So contaminated mine waste water wouldn’t just be pumped into a new mega dam. The mining company wanted to construct two separate processing plants to extract sulphuric acid and uranium from the existing tailings dams. This means they would be “mining” gold, sulphuric acid and uranium – keeping the gold and getting rid of the sulphuric acid and selling the uranium. The result? “Clean” mine waste water that could even be repurposed for eg, irrigation. Environmental groups were very excited. Finally the mining industry was taking their responsibility towards the environment seriously. So the construction of the dam started. Environmental impact studies were done – all based on the assumption that those two treatment plants would be constructed. The plans were approved by the then regulator, which was the Department of Agriculture, Conservation & Environment in North West. From the docs it seem that they regulator wasn’t that strict, because everyone was planning around a “clean” tailings dam. In fact, the dam was built on the banks of the Vaal River, because after the tailings were treated, there wasn’t much left that posed a threat to the environment. The dam wall was also not built with terraces as usual, because a clean dam didn’t pose as much of a risk as a toxic one. Note that the North West Department’s Authorisation did include a clause, saying: “Any changes to, or deviations from, the project description set out in this authorisation must be approved in writing by the Department, before such changes or deviations may be effected”. The project description obviously includes the building of the two extra treatment plants. Fast-forward to AngloGold’s promises: • the uranium extraction plant was built in 2014/2015 – and then the uranium market collapsed. The plant went out of operation within a year. • The sulphuric acid extraction plant was never built. In 2012 there were major spillages on the adjacent farms. Mariette Liefferink lay criminal charges against AngloGold, because of it. In 2017 there was ‘n spillage. Cyclone Dineo caused a lot of rain in the area and the dam had overflown – all hard and toxic metals right into the Vaal. We know mines more often than not, overpromise and underdeliver, but in 2019 a new impact study revealed that “the sulphate plume (polluted underground water table) at Kareerand continues to grow at a significant rate”. This is their heritage in SA. Not those cute slogans about caring about the environment and the communities. They came here, mined and left us with the damage. In 2020 Harmony Gold bought AngloGold’s South African assets. It was time to renew regulatory stuff. By that time, the DMRE has taken over from the provincial departments as regulator. Everything was approved once again. In 2021 Harmony Gold applied for a new water use licence with the Department of Water and Sanitation. The DWS flagged the issue with the dam and insisted that it gets lined. The crux: Harmony got approvals to continue working on a site that’s currently one of the biggest environmental threats in the country. There’s a chance that Harmony doesn’t know about AngloGold’s undelivered promises, but I strongly doubt it. AngloGold Ashanti deceived everyone (or bribed their way through) regulatory processes to make money. These environmental crimes can land people in prison. They have erected a tailings dam that, by the looks of the pictures I’ve seen, cannot handle the mass of polluted water it’s holding. The groundwater is so contaminated, that farmers apparently can’t use it. The interception boreholes drilled to control the mess underground, are few and far between, and those I’ve seen, are broken or overwhelmed by all the water. The DMRE and Water and Sanitation are either in on it, or blissfully unaware and will be sitting with egg on their faces for approving licences without proper review. According to my source, the dam wall is also not built according to regulations for a highly toxic tailings dam. And it’s already spilling in places. If it breaks, it will be the Merriespruit Disaster times 10, because of its size. This toxic dam is right next to the Vaal River. It’s already contaminating one of SA’s most important water resources, by spilling into the Koekemoerspruit. The Vaal River provides water to 19 million South Africans.
